title: Instructional Illusions with Carl Hendrick, Paul Kirschner and Jim Heal
author: Holly Korbey
summary: Holly Korbey replays her interview with Paul Kirschner, Jim Heal and Carl Hendrick about their book Instructional Illusions, which targets practices that look like good teaching on the surface but obscure what is happening in students' minds. They work through three illusions in turn. On engagement, they argue that what matters is cognitive engagement, not busy hands, and that memorable lessons often leave students remembering the episode rather than the content. On motivation, they say success produces motivation rather than the reverse, so small steps of experienced competence are the teacher's lever. On student-centered versus teacher-led instruction, they call the binary a caricature, note that constructivism describes how minds work rather than how to teach, and argue that explicit teacher direction that attends to prior knowledge is itself the most student-centered approach. The shared thread is that learning is a change in long-term memory, and that teachers who understand this can see through fads and gimmicks.
points: An instructional illusion is a practice whose surface features, such as busy and happy students, mask whether anything is being learned.
Engagement only counts when it is cognitive, so a silent class that is thinking can be a better lesson than a noisy, active one.
Motivation follows experiences of success, so teachers should break material into small steps that let students feel competent early.
The student-centered versus teacher-led debate is a false binary: constructivism is a theory of mind, and good teachers use prior knowledge and explicit schemas while directing instruction.
Memorable theatrics, like a teacher dressed as a Roman centurion, are weak evidence of learning when students cannot say what idea they were meant to learn.
quotes: Sometimes what we think works is not only different to what really works, but can often be sort of diametrically opposed to what actually the surface might seem.
A lot of education is done on vibes. In other words, I feel like I'm doing a really good thing. The kids are feeling like they're having a good time, so what's the problem?
Engagement is necessary, but it's about cognitive engagement, being engaged in your head with what you're learning, not with your hands.
They remembered the surface phenomena rather than the underlying architecture of the idea.
But if you're motivated to do something and you fail constantly at it, you're going to lose that motivation very quickly.
Constructivism isn't a theory of teaching, but rather a theory of how the mind works. And yet we have taken it to mean that students ought to construct their own learning.

The reality is that we need to allow students to think critically, but they can't think critically about nothing. We need to provide them with the building blocks and then provide them with the agency to make sense of them and build knowledge accordingly.

The most student-centered teaching that I can think of is teacher-directed, because the teacher is the expert who understands what the student is, what the student means, how the student should receive the material, then tailors the teaching to that.
